interactive.whatAmILookingAt: Twelve small screens share one grid and one solid arrow. The arrow runs from its tail at the origin to its tip. Its two parts are drawn dashed, nose to tail. The across part runs along the x-axis. The up part climbs from there to the tip. They meet at a right angle. So they close a right-angled triangle, with the arrow as its long side. A readout shows the parts as a column and as i and j. Here i is the unit vector along the x-axis. And j is the unit vector up the y-axis. Dragging the tip changes the arrow, and the dashed parts follow it. Given a size and an angle, the triangle gives the parts. The side next to the angle is the size times the angle's cosine. The side opposite is the size times its sine. A label on each dashed side says which. North is up the page and east is along the x-axis. A switch moves the angle marker from off the x-axis to a bearing. A bearing is measured clockwise from north. The arrow and its parts stay put. The same angle shows again at the tip, where the north part meets the arrow. So the cos label moves to the north side. Going back, the size is Pythagoras on the parts. A 3-D switch tips the grid back into a floor. A third axis, z, stands up at right angles to it. Its unit vector is k. The arrow stands in a box whose edges are its i, j and k parts. Dragging turns the box. The size is Pythagoras twice: across the floor, then up. The screens, in order: arrow a, 3 across and 4 up. A puzzle on an arrow 4 across and 2 down. A 10 N pull at 30° off the x-axis, with an angle slider from 0° to 90°. A puzzle on a 20 N pull at 60°. The bearing switch on the 10 N pull. A puzzle on 12 knots on a bearing of 030. The arrow −3i + 4j and its angle. A puzzle on the size of 5i − 12j. The box for 2i + 3j + 6k. A puzzle on the size of 4i + 4j + 7k. Two mixed puzzles: a ring on one rope with its parts drawn, and a 50 N winch rope on a bearing of 120. Some screens show an idea. The rest ask you to try it. Each puzzle offers three answers. A wrong pick is drawn, so you can see where it goes wrong.
interactive.ignores: The grid's squares have no unit. So one arrow can stand for newtons, knots or metres. Here the parts always lie along the x and y axes. But a vector can be split along any two lines at right angles, such as along and across a slope. Turning the 3-D box changes only your view. The arrow and its parts stay the same. The puzzles use example values. Parts are rounded to two decimal places.

explain.text:
A vector on a flat page splits into two parts at right angles, one along each axis. These parts are its [[component]]s: the separate x and y values of the vector. Take arrow a again, 3 across and 4 up. Its across part runs along the x-axis. Its up part climbs from there to the tip. Drawn nose to tail, the two parts end exactly at the arrow's tip. So together they are the arrow itself, described along the axes. They are not extra pulls. The two parts and the arrow close a right-angled triangle. The arrow is its long side. You can write the parts as a column, 3 above 4. Or you can write them as 3i + 4j. Here i is the unit vector along the x-axis. And j is the unit vector up the y-axis. So 3i + 4j means 3 lots of i, then 4 lots of j.

Often you know the size and an angle instead. Then the triangle gives you the parts. Take a 10 N pull at 30° above the x-axis. The angle sits between the arrow and the across side. In a right-angled triangle, the side next to an angle is the long side times the angle's cosine. So the across part is 10 cos 30° = 8.66 N. The side opposite the angle is the long side times its sine. So the up part is 10 sin 30° = 5 N. Finding the parts this way is called [[resolving]] the pull. Each part is shorter than the arrow, unless the arrow lies along an axis. Then one part is the whole arrow and the other is zero. A bearing shows why it matters which side sits next to the angle. Put north up the page and east along the x-axis. A bearing is measured clockwise from north. The pull sits 30° above east. So it is 60° round from north: a bearing of 060. Now the angle sits next to the north side, so north takes the cosine: 10 cos 60° = 5 N. East takes the sine: 10 sin 60° = 8.66 N. The parts have not changed. Only the angle moved, and the cos moved with it.

To go back from the parts to the size, use Pythagoras. Never just add the parts. The pull's parts give √(8.66² + 5²) = 10 N, not 13.66 N. The angle comes from the tangent, but check the signs first. Take −3i + 4j. A calculator's tan⁻¹(4 ÷ −3) gives −53.13°. That points right and down. The signs say left and up, so add 180° to get 126.87°. A third axis, z, stands at right angles to both of the others. Its unit vector is k. The vector 2i + 3j + 6k runs 2 across, 3 along and 6 up. Across the floor, Pythagoras gives √(2² + 3²) = √13. The 6 up stands at right angles to that floor line. So Pythagoras again gives √(13 + 6²) = √49 = 7. Parts along one axis add and take away as plain numbers.[^1] That is what makes adding vectors easy.

**A vector's components are its parts along the axes, written ai + bj + ck. The part next to the given angle is the size times its cosine. The other part is the size times its sine. Pythagoras on the parts gives back the size.**

analogy.text: Your power triangle is the same split. Say a load draws 10 kVA at a power factor of 0.8. The active power is the side next to the angle φ: 10 × 0.8 = 8 kW. When cos φ is 0.8, sin φ is 0.6. The reactive power is the side opposite, so it is 10 × 0.6 = 6 kvar. Pythagoras takes you back to 10 kVA. Adding them, 8 + 6 = 14, means nothing.
analogy.breaks: The angle φ is a shift in time between current and voltage. It is not a direction in space. So the power triangle has no third axis and nothing like k.

practice.text:
- Draw the arrow and its two parts nose to tail. They close a right-angled triangle.
- Mark the given angle. The side next to it is the size times cos. The other side is the size times sin.
- With an angle off the x-axis, across is size × cos θ and up is size × sin θ. With a bearing, east is size × sin θ and north is size × cos θ.
- Give each part its sign. Left, down, west and south are all minus.
- Check that Pythagoras on the parts gives back the size.
- To get back to an angle, use the tangent. Then check the quarter from the signs.

**Rule of thumb:** Cos goes on the side next to the angle.

**Worked example:** A submarine makes 8 knots on a bearing of 210. East is 8 sin 210° = −4 knots. North is 8 cos 210° = −6.93 knots. So its velocity is −4i − 6.93j. Both parts are minus, so it heads south and west, as a bearing of 210 should. Check: √(4² + 6.93²) gives back 8 knots, to rounding.

**Common mistakes**
- Putting sin next to the angle. With a bearing, the angle sits next to north, so north takes cos.
- Giving a part the arrow's whole size. That only happens when the arrow lies along that axis.
- Adding the parts to get the size. 5i − 12j has size 13, not 17.
- Writing the parts the wrong way round. 4i − 2j is 4 across and 2 down. It is not −2i + 4j.
- Trusting tan⁻¹ without checking the signs. −3i + 4j points at 126.87°, not −53.13°.
- Leaving k out of the size. 4i + 4j + 7k has size 9.
- Counting the parts as extra pulls. A ring on one rope feels one pull.

sources.quote: Vector components describe the separate x, y and z values of a vector. When working with vectors, components can be added or subtracted separately.

interactive.html:
Most screens show an arrow on a grid, its two parts dashed beside it and written out on the right. The pulls, the ship and the winch rope are made-up examples.

The side next to the angle takes the cosine. Pythagoras on the parts gives back the size.

checks.label: Vector components describe the separate x, y and z values of a vector: the readout's column lists arrow a's x and y values and the box arrow's x, y and z values, the same numbers as their i, j and k parts, and drawn nose to tail those parts end at the tip
Dragging the tip sets the parts: for every square the tip can reach, the column and the i and j readout give its across and up moves, and the dashed parts still end at the tip

At every whole angle from 0° to 90° the 10 N pull resolves into 10 cos θ across and 10 sin θ up: the readout shows both to two decimal places, the cos label sits on the across side next to the angle, each part is shorter than 10 N unless the pull lies along an axis, and Pythagoras on the parts gives back 10 N

Switching the 10 N pull to a bearing moves only the angle and its labels: the arrow, its parts and its column stay the same, the angle reads 30° off the x-axis and then a bearing of 060, the same 60° shows at the tip where the north part meets the arrow, and the cos label moves from the across side to the north side

With a bearing the angle sits next to north, so north takes the cosine: the ship's and the winch rope's pictures mark the bearing again at the tip, on the north part, and their right answers put cos on that side, giving 12 sin 30° = 6 knots east, and 43.3 N east with −25 N north; the winch's wrong picks point on bearings 150 and 060

Every number in the puzzles follows from the rule: 20 cos 60° = 10 and 20 sin 60° = 17.32; 12 cos 30° = 10.39; √(25 + 144) = 13 against 5 + 12 = 17 and 5 − 12 = −7; √13 = 3.61 and √49 = 7; √32 = 5.66, 4 + 4 + 7 = 15 and √81 = 9
A calculator's tan⁻¹(4 ÷ −3) gives −53.13°, pointing right and down, the opposite way to −3i + 4j; turned through 180° it lands on the arrow at 126.87°, and Pythagoras gives its size, 5

Turning the box changes only the view: at every turn from −55° to −10° its parts still run 2 across, 3 along and 6 up, nose to tail to the tip, the floor line reads 3.61 and the size 7, while the tip moves on the page
Every puzzle offers three different answers with exactly one accepted, gives each wrong one its own hint, and draws a wrong pick in red but a right one without
Before Check no puzzle's picture shows its answer, and a right answer shows it
Every demonstration has finished arriving within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion within 2.5 s

applied.problem: "Any vector can be split into two parts" is false for the 3-D vectors this same lesson and the cross product (i6) use, which need three parts, i, j and k; narrowed to a vector on a flat page.
The worked example check writes √(4² + 6.93²) = √64, but 16 + 6.93² is 64.02; the rounded part only gives back 8 knots to rounding, so the equals sign is false precision.
